content: Argemone mexicana, commonly known as the Mexican Poppy, Mexican Prickly Poppy, or Cardo Santo, is a species of poppy native to Mexico. It has since become widely naturalized in regions such as the United States and India. This plant is an annual herb characterized by its bright yellow sap, which has been traditionally utilized by indigenous populations in the western United States and parts of Mexico. When the seed pods of Argemone mexicana are cut open, they release a pale-yellow latex substance. This latex, referred to as Argemone resin, contains the alkaloids berberine and protopine, which have medicinal properties and are used as sedatives. The seeds of this plant contain 22-36% of a pale yellow, non-edible oil known as Argemone oil or Katkar oil. This oil is toxic due to the presence of alkaloids such as sanguinarine and dihydrosanguinarine. The seeds of Argemone mexicana closely resemble those of Brassica nigra (mustard), which can lead to the unintentional or deliberate adulteration of mustard seeds with Argemone seeds, rendering the product poisonous. Despite its toxicity, Argemone oil has been used medicinally to treat conditions such as dropsy, jaundice, and various skin diseases. However, poisoning from Katkar oil can result in a condition known as epidemic dropsy, which is characterized by severe swelling, particularly in the legs. Several significant cases of Katkar oil poisoning have been reported in countries such as India, Fiji, and South Africa. The most recent major outbreak in India occurred in 1998. Research has shown that even a 1% adulteration of mustard oil with Argemone oil can lead to clinical disease. Additionally, extracts from this plant are marketed online as an herbal alternative to marijuana.
